nutshell: Medical image re-identification (MedReID) - matching scans/images of the same patient, useful for retrieving a patient's historical records and for detecting/removing identity-leaking visual cues before data sharing - has only been studied per-modality (e.g. just X-ray or just fundus) so far. This paper proposes MaMI, a single model that handles many medical modalities (X-ray, CT, MRI, fundus, histopathology) at once via a per-image adaptive parameter module, further regularized by aligning it with pretrained medical foundation models on inter-image feature differences, and validates it across an 11-dataset benchmark plus two downstream applications.
contributions: Continuous modality-based Parameter Adapter (ComPA): rather than a discrete modality label (X-ray=0, CT=1, ...), each image is mapped to a continuous 'modality context' constrained to a learned 32-entry basis codebook, which then generates low-rank, grouped (LoRA-style) parameters that adapt a shared modality-agnostic ViT backbone per-image at runtime - shown to beat both single-modality specialist models and naive multi-modality fine-tuning, which the paper shows actually degrades X-ray accuracy relative to a specialist model (94.21% -> 92.30%, Table 1).

Medical-prior transfer via inter-image difference alignment: learnable modality-specific query tokens select 'key features' from both MaMI and a frozen, per-modality medical foundation model (MFM), and instead of aligning single-image features, the model aligns the *difference* between a pair of images' key features via a contrastive loss - motivated by ReID being inherently about discriminating pairs; the ablation (Table 8) shows this beats global-feature, non-selected, and single-image-alignment variants.

An 11-dataset, cross-modality MedReID benchmark (X-ray, CT, MRI, fundus, histopathology) evaluating 25 foundation models and 8 large multimodal language models, plus two downstream demonstrations: retrieval-augmented diagnosis (using MaMI to pull a patient's relevant historical images with no identity labels, improving diagnostic accuracy) and privacy protection (a U-Net trained to strip identity-revealing visual cues while preserving disease-classification utility).
deficiencies: The privacy-protection application (Table 4) still leaves MaMI itself able to re-identify 21.23% of protected Chest-X images (down from 91.49% unprotected) - a real reduction, but not a strong guarantee - and is only tested on one dataset, with the identity-removal network trained on a different dataset (MIMIC-X) than it's evaluated on; there's no cross-dataset or cross-modality test of the privacy tool itself, despite privacy protection being one of only two headline applications.

The claim that privacy-protected images 'preserve the data utility well' rests on a single pair of disease-classification numbers (81.24% original vs. 80.67% protected, Sec 4.3) with no per-class breakdown, no variance/repeated-run reporting, and no comparison against a naive baseline (e.g. simple cropping/blurring of identity-linked regions) to show the learned removal is actually better than trivial redaction.

The most striking single result - cross-modality patient linking, X-ray to CT association at 94.38% after tuning (Table 3) - is evaluated on a single unreleased 'licensed private dataset' of 1814 patients, so this capability can't be independently verified or reproduced from the paper alone.

MaMI's margin over the strongest fine-tuned single-modality/general baselines is large on small, data-scarce datasets (e.g. HCC-TACE: 211 total scans, MaMI 88.09% vs. best baseline ~80%) but much smaller on the largest dataset (MIMIC-X: 111K images, MaMI 96.89% vs. CLIP† 92.30%, TransReID† 86.80%) - the 'consistently superior' framing doesn't distinguish between a genuine all-in-one advantage and a 'helps most when data is scarce' story, which the ablation results (Table 5, MFM alignment mattering most on the smallest dataset) actually support.

Dataset sizes and gallery/query splits vary enormously across the 11 benchmark datasets (211 scans for HCC-TACE vs. 111,333 images for MIMIC-X) but the paper never reports per-dataset identity counts or gallery sizes used for the CMC-R1 metric, making it hard to judge how comparable a 71% Rank-1 on one dataset is to a 97% Rank-1 on another.
notable: MaMI is explicitly dual-use by its own framing: the same model is presented as both a tool for linking a patient's medical history across poorly-organized/cross-institutional records (identification) and a tool for detecting and removing identity cues (de-identification) - but a model this effective at cross-modality, cross-institution patient linking (94.38% X-ray-to-CT accuracy after tuning) is also a strong de-anonymization tool if misused, and the paper releases code/model with no discussion of access controls or misuse risk despite this tension being central to its own stated motivation. Separately notable: the benchmark finds masked-image-modeling backbones (MAE, MaskFeat) perform far worse zero-shot than contrastive backbones (MoCoV3, DINOv2) on medical images - 19.95%/68.33% vs. 84-91% Rank-1 on Lung-CT - but end up matching or beating the contrastive models after fine-tuning on most datasets, a specific empirical data point about pretraining-objective transfer behavior that's reusable well beyond this paper's own MedReID contribution.
